modelNote: The one fact everything turns on. Three positions the Whatcom co-op could take, what each one unlocks, what each one costs, what kind of workbench each one implies, and how each one fails. The middle position is the one reachable without an insurance licence. Drawn Aug 16 2026.

legendEntries.label: A position the co-op could take

nodes.label: WHAT DOES THE CO-OP HOLD?
nodes.note: Everything downstream turns on this single fact. It settles whether the workbench is a coordination system or a contracting system — and those are different products, not different phases of one product.

nodes.label: CONVENE
nodes.note: Holds relationships, convening power and a shared table. Holds no money and no contract.

nodes.label: CONTRACT AS AGENT
nodes.note: Pooled self-funded employers appoint the co-op as their contracting agent. The employers bear the claims risk they already bear today; the co-op controls plan design and who gets paid for what. This is the counterparty position WITHOUT an insurance licence — and the broker in your founding group is the person who knows whether it can be assembled here.

nodes.label: BEAR RISK
nodes.note: The co-op becomes a licensed risk-bearing entity and holds the premium outright.

nodes.label: Shared measures · a shared care plan · comparison between providers · trust
nodes.note: Real value, and not nothing — a shared plan and agreed measures are preconditions for everything else. But every item here is something the co-op can produce by persuasion, which is exactly why none of it changes behaviour that is being paid to go the other way.

nodes.label: Cannot change what is paid for · cannot require verification · cannot open an order to bidders · cannot end an arrangement that is not working
nodes.note: This is the list that matters. Each line is a capability that requires holding money, and no amount of goodwill substitutes for one of them. A convener asking a health system to change what it charges for is asking a favour; a purchaser is placing an order.

nodes.label: A COORDINATION SYSTEM — shared plan, identity, measures. No settlement, so no teeth.
nodes.note: Not a lesser version of the contracting system — a genuinely different product. Shared plan, shared identity, shared measures, and no settlement. Build this believing it will grow into the other one and you will build the wrong data model, because a coordination system has no order register and no ledger.

nodes.label: Everyone agrees. Nothing changes. It produces a report.
nodes.note: The specific failure mode of every health improvement collaborative: high-quality agreement, a published report, and a baseline that does not move. Worth naming in advance so it is recognisable early rather than at year three.

nodes.label: Defines the dān · contracts directly with care teams · pays on the member's verification · opens an order to whoever can meet it · can exit a provider
nodes.note: The counterparty capabilities, all of which follow from the single fact of holding the money. Note the last one: the ability to END an arrangement is what makes the other four credible.

nodes.label: Needs a pool of self-funded employers, a TPA or settlement rail, stop-loss cover, plan-design control, and a health lawyer on Stark and anti-kickback before the contracts are drafted
nodes.note: The real bill of materials. The lawyer is listed deliberately: Stark and anti-kickback constrain precisely the shape wanted here — outcome-contingent payments moving between parties who also refer to each other — and that has to shape the instruments before they are drafted, not after.

nodes.label: A CONTRACTING SYSTEM — order register, VAM contracts, member verification, settlement ledger, win-win statement
nodes.note: Five components. The order register and the verification are the two nobody else has built; the ledger, contracts and statement all have precedents to borrow from.

nodes.label: Employers leave the pool after the first bad year, and the pool was the whole leverage.
nodes.note: The pool is the entire leverage, and a pool is voluntary. One bad claims year and employers can walk, which means stop-loss cover is not a technicality — it is what buys the experiment enough time to show anything.

nodes.label: Holds the whole premium · sets the price · keeps the savings · answers to members only
nodes.note: Everything the agent position unlocks, plus the price and the surplus. Strictly more power, at a cost most co-ops cannot pay for years.

nodes.label: Insurance licence · reserves · actuarial capability · state regulator · years, and capital you do not have yet
nodes.note: Reserves and licensure are the hard gates; the softer one is actuarial capability, which is a skill set rather than a purchase and takes as long to build as the capital takes to raise.

nodes.label: A CONTRACTING SYSTEM plus an insurer's whole back office
nodes.note: The same workbench as the middle path, sitting under a claims operation, a compliance function and a reserve calculation. The workbench is not the hard part of this position.

nodes.label: Becomes the carrier it set out to replace, and re-learns why carriers behave that way.
nodes.note: Not a moral failing. Carriers behave the way they do because holding downside risk on a population produces those behaviours, and a co-op holding the same risk will feel the same pressures from its own board.

nodes.label: The middle position is the reachable one: it buys the counterparty seat without buying a licence.
nodes.note: Stated as a judgement, not a fact. What makes it testable: the broker in the founding group can establish in an afternoon whether enough self-funded employers exist locally to form a pool. That single question gates the whole design.
